CausalChain: HCC cells under hypoxia -> HIF-1α upregulates ENTPD2 and promotes exosomal ncRNA release -> ENTPD2 converts extracellular ATP to 5′ AMP -> Increased 5′ AMP (and exosomal ncRNAs) enhance recruitment/activation of MDSCs -> MDSCs suppress T cell function and enhance immunosuppression -> Reduced T cell antitumor activity leads to poor ICI response -> Dual inhibition (via ENTPD2 silencing and exosome disruption) diminishes MDSC accumulation -> Restored T cell function enhances ICI efficacy in HCC
Hypothesis: In HCC, a dual intervention strategy that concurrently targets HIF-1α-driven ENTPD2 expression and exosome-mediated ncRNA signaling will more effectively disrupt the ATP-to-5′ AMP conversion process and subsequent recruitment/activation of MDSCs than targeting ENTPD2 alone. Implementation involves using CRISPR/dCas9-based epigenetic silencing to downregulate ENTPD2 and nanocarrier-based inhibitors to block exosomal communication. Such a combined approach is hypothesized to alleviate immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment and synergize with immune checkpoint blockade therapies, thereby improving clinical outcomes.
Abstract: We propose a dual-targeted therapeutic strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) that integrates metabolic modulation with immunotherapy enhancement. Building on the established causal chain linking hypoxia to HIF-1α mediated upregulation of ENTPD2 and subsequent ATP-to-5′ AMP conversion, our hypothesis refines the original concept by simultaneously targeting ENTPD2 and exosome-mediated immunomodulatory signaling. This combined approach employs state-of-the-art CRISPR/dCas9 epigenetic silencing to reduce HIF-1α‐driven ENTPD2 expression and utilizes nanocarrier-mediated delivery of exosome inhibitors to disrupt non-coding RNA (ncRNA) communication in the tumor microenvironment. By mitigating the accumulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and thereby reducing immunosuppression, this strategy is expected to restore T cell antitumor function and enhance the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapies in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that targeting ENTPD2 to block the ATP-to-5′ AMP conversion would reduce MDSC recruitment and enhance checkpoint blockade efficacy. The revised hypothesis retains this core concept but enriches it by incorporating additional established elements – namely HIF-1α’s role in upregulating ENTPD2 under hypoxic conditions and the contribution of exosomal ncRNAs to immunosuppressive cell activation. Technologically, the new hypothesis leverages CRISPR/dCas9 epigenetic silencing and nanocarrier-mediated exosome inhibition, thus rendering the approach more robust and aligned with current research capabilities. Each causal step – from hypoxia-induced ENTPD2 expression and extracellular nucleotide conversion to MDSC-mediated immunosuppression – is explicitly addressed and integrated into a multi-layered intervention strategy.
